title: The Aymara Kingdoms
titleline: The Aymara Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Aymara Kingdoms. The Aymara kingdoms - also called the lake kingdoms - developed between 1150 and 1477 CE in the high plateau around Lake Titicaca, in the region Andeans called Qullaw, after the disappearance of Tiwanaku left a political vacuum. In its wake, a number of Aymara-speaking, independent, and rival kingdoms emerged, among them the Lupaca, the Colla, the Pacajes, and the Azangaros. Their world was divided between Urcosuyu - 'male, fire' - on the western side of the lake and Umasuyu - 'female, water' - on the eastern side, and their societies often had two leaders apiece; most of these kingdoms buried their leaders in tower-shaped mausoleums, and each held lands at different altitudes in what scholars call a 'vertical archipelago'. These kingdoms matter because they kept the Andean altiplano's ancient ways alive through the centuries between empires, and their lords would play decisive roles in the fate of the Inca.
para2: The kingdoms warred constantly - above all the rivalry between the Aymara kurakas of Chucuito, of the Lupaca kingdom, and Hatunqulla, of the Colla kingdom. When the Inca pressed south, the Lupaca leader Cari faced the Colla leader Chuqui Capac, who attacked the Lupacas near Paucarcolla before the Inca army arrived; after a long battle near Hatunqulla, Chuqui Capac was taken prisoner, and the Colla lands were subdued - some by force, others peacefully. Destroyed towns were repopulated with mitmakunas, resettled colonists, and the Aymara kingdoms accepted the dominion of Cuzco while keeping their lands and their far-off colonies in the eastern mountains. That arrangement survived until the first years of the Spanish conquest, when the kingdoms' territorial and political dismemberment began.
source2label: Smithsonian Institution: The Great Inka Road: Engineering an Empire

title: The Chimú Empire
titleline: The Chimú Empire - The History Web
para1: The Chimu Empire. The Chimu were the largest and most prosperous culture of the Late Intermediate Period along the Peruvian coast, flourishing between the 12th and 15th centuries CE with their capital at the great city of Chan Chan. The Chimu constructed cities and developed large-scale irrigation systems using canals, and there seems to have been much social stratification. Rulers like Guacricaur expanded into the Moche, Santa, and Zana valleys, and in 1375 CE, under Nancinpinco, the Chimu conquered the Lambayeque (Sican) culture, absorbing some of its cultural practices; tribute extracted through successful military campaigns and political coercion made them the dominant regional power, with Chan Chan the capital of administrative centers across the valleys. This empire matters because it was the last great coastal civilization before the Inca, and its methods - in administration, craft, and imperial organization - were studied by its conquerors.
para2: The Chimu spoke the Yunca language - also called Mochica or Moche - now extinct and definitely distinct from the Inca tongue, and they produced characteristic black ware ceramics. Their imperial system was sophisticated: conquered rulers were allowed a certain autonomy, and compounds of foreign artisans were gathered in the capital, a policy the Inca would later adopt. The empire's independence ended when the Inca, under Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui and his son Topa Inca Yupanqui, conquered it between 1465 and 1470 CE, capturing the 11th known Chimu ruler, Minchancaman, around 1470; thereafter the Chimu became a vassal state within the Inca Empire. Yet the story does not end there - the imperial playbook the Inca inherited, from road-fed tribute to artisan compounds, carried the imprint of the coastal kingdom it had absorbed.
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 4.2.11.1: Introduction to the Chimú culture

title: The Inca Empire (Tahuantinsuyu)
titleline: The Inca Empire (Tahuantinsuyu) - The History Web
para1: The Inca Empire: Tahuantinsuyu. The Inca Empire, known to its people as Tahuantinsuyu - 'The Four Parts Together' - arose sometime in the early 1400s and became the largest indigenous empire of the Americas. How much of that growth owes to a single great leader, an Alexander-the-Great-like Pachacuti? Scholars note the Incas had been developing the capability for conquest over four to six generations, though the 1586 chronicle of the Spanish cleric Miguel Cabello Valboa dates Pachacuti's reign to 1438-1471 and his son Tupac Inca Yupanqui's to the years that followed. The empire matters because it bound the Andes into a single administered world, from imperial Cuzco outward, through a system of administration and infrastructure unmatched anywhere in the pre-Columbian Americas.
para2: At the heart of that system was a vast network of roads - some 40,000 kilometers according to John Hyslop, the leading scholar of the subject - built to move armies and administrative resources across a hugely varied landscape, connecting the capital to provincial centers, with many smaller branches extending to outposts east and west; the roads varied in width and style because Inca leaders often utilized existing routes. Around Cuzco, workers received their food from state storehouses every four days or even daily, and below the emperor, religious officials and magistrates called kurakas oversaw the day-to-day administration of their regions, collecting taxes, overseeing day-to-day administration, and even choosing brides for the men of their communities. The empire's end came swiftly: after a devastating civil war between the half-brothers Atahualpa and Huascar, the Spaniard Pizarro captured and executed Atahualpa, dealing a fatal blow to what had been the largest indigenous empire of the Americas.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Pizarro & the Fall of the Inca Empire
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 12.21: Administration of the Inca Empire

title: The Muisca Confederation
titleline: The Muisca Confederation - The History Web
para1: The Muisca Confederation. The Muisca civilization flourished in the fertile eastern highlands of what is now Colombia between 600 and 1600 CE, its territory encompassing modern Bogota and its environs, and it has gained lasting fame as the origin of the legend of El Dorado - 'The Gilded One'. A Muisca ceremony held at Lake Guatavita - actually only one of many kinds - involved a ruler being covered in gold dust; the Spanish, hearing this story, allowed their imagination and lust for gold to leap beyond the bounds of reality, and soon a legend arose of a magnificent golden kingdom. This confederation matters because its goldwork is among the great artistic traditions of the Americas: for the Muisca, gold was not used as a currency but as an artistic medium, mined from exposed veins and panned from mountain rivers.
para2: The Muisca goldsmiths employed a wide range of techniques - lost-wax casting, a two-tone finish, repousse, soldering, granulation, and filigree - and hammered gold into thin sheets on round stone anvils. Their tunjos - small votive figures of snakes and flat male, female, and animal forms in gold alloy - were placed at sacred sites, and elite members of society wore pectorals, earrings, and nose studs. Nor did they restrict their art to gold: they created fine textiles of wool or cotton. There is ample evidence that commodities such as gold, shells, feathers, animal skins, tobacco, salt, and coca leaves moved through Muisca markets in a thriving regional trade. When the Spanish arrived in the 1530s, drawn by the very legend the Muisca had inspired, this rich highland world was drawn into the colonial age.
source3label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Northern Andes, 1400–1600 A.D.

title: The Chachapoya Culture
titleline: The Chachapoya Culture - The History Web
para1: The Chachapoya, called the Warriors of the Clouds by the Inca, built some of the most spectacular cities in the Americas on misty mountaintops in northern Peru. Their homeland lay in the cloud forests of the eastern Andes, where ridges rise above the Utcubamba River valley and rain feeds dense forests draped in orchids and bromeliads. From about 800 CE, Chachapoya communities constructed settlements of circular stone houses decorated with geometric friezes in zigzag and diamond patterns, a style found nowhere else in the Andes.
para2: The greatest Chachapoya monument is Kuélap, a walled fortress-city perched on a limestone ridge at three thousand meters. Its outer wall rises up to twenty meters high and stretches for hundreds of meters, pierced by only three narrow entrance passages that funnel into steep ramps, easy to defend. Inside, more than four hundred circular buildings housed a population of several thousand. Kuélap was once thought to be purely a fortress, but archaeologists now see it as a political and ceremonial center for the surrounding region, occupied for centuries and remodeled many times.
para3: Chachapoya society was organized in local chiefdoms rather than a single kingdom, and the cloud forest peoples farmed terraced fields of maize, potatoes, and beans, raised llamas, and traded with the coast and the Amazon lowlands. They buried their dead in spectacular fashion, placing mummies in chullpas, small burial houses built into cliff faces, and in the famous sarcophagi of Karajía, two-meter-tall clay figures perched on a cliff ledge that once held mummy bundles. Spanish chroniclers later described the Chachapoya as tall and fair-skinned, giving rise to fanciful legends of lost European tribes, but archaeology shows they were a local Andean people.
para4: In the 1470s the Inca emperor Topa Inca Yupanqui conquered the Chachapoya after hard fighting, deporting many thousands under the Inca resettlement system. When the Spanish arrived decades later, some Chachapoya allied with them against the Inca, and the region became a base for early Spanish expeditions toward the Amazon. Kuélap, once known as the Machu Picchu of the north, is now a major archaeological park reached by cable car, and ongoing excavations continue to reveal the sophistication of this cloud-forest civilization.

title: The Tairona and the Sierra Nevada Chiefdoms
titleline: The Tairona and the Sierra Nevada Chiefdoms - The History Web
para1: The Tairona civilization flourished on the Caribbean slopes of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta in Colombia, building stone cities on jungle ridges and crafting some of the finest goldwork of the ancient Americas. From the early centuries CE, Tairona communities terraced the steep mountainsides of the world's highest coastal mountain range, creating a network of stone-paved paths, plazas, stairways, and circular house platforms. At its height around 1000-1500 CE, the Tairona population may have numbered in the hundreds of thousands across the Sierra Nevada's northern slopes.
para2: The most famous Tairona site is Ciudad Perdida, the Lost City, known to the local Kogi people as Teyuna. Built from about 800 CE, it consists of over two hundred stone terraces linked by stairways, crowning a ridge deep in the forest. It was rediscovered by looters in the 1970s, sparking a treasure rush before the government secured the site. Other major centers included Pueblito and Bonda. Tairona towns were connected by stone roads that ran along the ridgelines, parts of which still survive and are used by Indigenous communities today.
para3: Tairona artisans were master goldsmiths, working in the lost-wax technique to cast intricate pendants of bat-men, jaguars, and shamans in tumbaga, a gold-copper alloy. Their ceramics included incised blackware jars, and they carved stone batons, beads, and ceremonial seats. Tairona religion centered on the Sierra Nevada itself, regarded as the heart of the world, with priests maintaining cosmic balance through ritual. This worldview survives strikingly intact among the Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa, and Kankuamo peoples, the Tairona's direct descendants, who still farm the same terraces and walk the same stone paths.
para4: Spanish contact brought catastrophe. Coastal Tairona towns were drawn into the pearl and slave trades, and from the 1520s Spanish expeditions pushed inland, meeting stiff resistance. After decades of war, the surviving Tairona withdrew into the high Sierra, where their descendants preserved their traditions in isolation for centuries. Today the Kogi and their neighbors are recognized as guardians of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, and Ciudad Perdida, reached by a multi-day jungle trek, has become one of South America's great archaeological destinations.
source4label: Journal of Field Archaeology: Tairona settlement research

title: The Mapuche before the Conquest
titleline: The Mapuche before the Conquest - The History Web
para1: The Mapuche, the people of the land, developed in the valleys and forests of south-central Chile into one of the most resilient Indigenous societies of the Americas. Their ancestors had inhabited the region for thousands of years, and by about 600 CE their communities were settling into farming life, cultivating maize, potatoes, quinoa, and beans and raising llamas. The Mapuche never formed a centralized state. Instead they lived in scattered, largely autonomous communities organized around extended families, each led by a lonko, or headman, with religious life guided by shamans called machi, usually women.
para2: Mapuche society was decentralized but far from primitive. Communities gathered for collective labor, feasts, games, and councils where disputes were settled and war leaders chosen. Their world stretched from the Itata River south toward Chiloé, encompassing coastal ranges, fertile central valleys, and the northern edges of the rainy southern forests. They traded with peoples of the Andes and the Argentine pampas, adopting technologies and ideas while fiercely guarding local independence. Silver work later became a Mapuche hallmark, with elaborate jewelry worn by women of status.
para3: The first empire to test Mapuche independence was the Inca. In the late fifteenth century, Inca armies pushed south through Chile, incorporating the northern valleys as far as the Maule River. At the Maule they met the Mapuche and their allies, and after a major battle, commonly placed around the 1470s-1480s, the Inca advance stopped. The Maule became a frontier: north of it lay the Inca province of Chile, south of it the unconquered Araucanía. The Mapuche learned from the encounter, adopting some Inca military and political ideas while rejecting Inca rule.
para4: When the Spanish arrived in the 1540s, they found no emperor to capture, only hundreds of determined communities. The Mapuche destroyed the first Spanish towns in the south and in 1553, under the toqui Lautaro, defeated and killed the conquistador Pedro de Valdivia. Thus began the Arauco War, which would burn for three centuries, the longest resistance in the Americas. The Mapuche remained independent in their heartland until the 1880s, and today they are the largest Indigenous people of Chile, still defending land and language.
source3label: Country Studies (Library of Congress): Chile: The Indigenous Population
